title: Cited conversational tax research assistant instead of keyword database search
problem: Advisers find legacy research databases slow, and general chatbots return confident citations that may not exist.
approach: Advisers ask in plain language and get answers with inline citations to primary authority; products include Blue J, Accordance and CoCounsel Tax.
Named users include Sasserath & Co., SSC CPAs, Sorren, RSM US and Harris, Hardy & Johnstone.
A 25-person firm reports simple research fell from 1 hour to 10 minutes (vendor-published).
The adviser opens and reads each cited authority; a reviewer tests the reasoning before it goes to a client.
who: Blue J, Accordance, Thomson Reuters, RSM US

title: Multi-step research plans for gray-area tax questions run in the adviser's session
problem: Hard gray-area questions took hours across several databases, and search tools still left substantial manual work to apply findings to a client.
approach: Accordance runs each step with dedicated agents; Bloomberg Tax announced a Deep Thinking Mode; Thomson Reuters calls CoCounsel Tax reason-and-act.
A CPA leading research at a 100-professional firm says two to six hours of research takes 15 or 20 minutes (vendor-published).
A senior researcher checks the plan and authority; a partner reviews before advice reaches the client.

title: Research agent works a question end to end, submitting a cited answer
problem: A corporate tax research question needs several chained lookups, and an early error in a threshold, date or citation carries through to the answer.
approach: An agent researches a written question over many steps and submits one cited answer; EY India announced research agents.
On the Vals AI Tax Agent Bench the top score was 49.19% as read 2026-10-17 (independent benchmark, not a firm deployment).
A qualified adviser reviews the memo and every authority before it reaches a client.

title: Idea: specialist state-by-state and multi-jurisdiction research workflow
problem: Idea, not a deployment: multi-jurisdiction questions such as 50-state surveys are where AI tools do worst and where manual work is longest.
approach: Idea: a purpose-built workflow searches each jurisdiction's primary law and compiles a comparison table for adviser review.
Vals suggests a specialist 50-state workflow should beat basic prompts; legal AI scored 14 points lower on multi-jurisdiction questions (independent).
The adviser verifies each jurisdiction's result against primary law.

title: Knowledge assistant over a firm's or department's own memos and precedents
problem: Institutional tax knowledge sits in senior practitioners' heads and scattered memos, and vendors say it is lost as seniors retire.
approach: An assistant answers from the organization's own memos and policies plus licensed content; Thomson Reuters markets CoCounsel Tax with a Knowledge Base.
KPMG's tax knowledge management leader joined a Bloomberg Tax forum panel on AI integration; no outcome figures are published (vendor-published).
A reviewer confirms a retrieved precedent still reflects current law and fits the client's facts.

title: In-house tax teams triage technical questions with licensed and enterprise AI assistants
problem: Corporate tax teams answer ad hoc technical questions with limited staff; 58% of departments surveyed by Thomson Reuters were under-resourced.
approach: KPMG Germany quick surveys found 89% use company-wide AI solutions and 29% specialised tax applications; teams are trialling CoCounsel and Accordance.
KPMG Germany says 66% of AI users report noticeable time savings, across all AI use (self-reported).
The tax director reviews AI-assisted conclusions before they go to the CFO, auditors or authorities.

title: Firm-wide approved research assistants, a named tax AI owner and governance
problem: Staff use general chatbots for tax questions whether or not approved, and large firms lack central control over what is pasted into which AI.
approach: The firm licenses one standard assistant, names an AI leader and trains staff; Crowe signed for Ask Blue J.
PwC has a US AI Tax Leader and reports over 3,200 AI champions (self-reported).
The managing partner or tax leader approves tools, and human review applies at each level.

title: AI-supported research training and coaching for junior staff
problem: Junior staff lack the background to navigate legacy research tools, and seniors act as informal research trainers.
approach: Firms use the cited research assistant as a tutor; Jansen & Company's senior managing director says he uses AI as a tutor.
Sasserath & Co. says younger staff did not unlearn legacy methods; Finney Neill says less experienced staff could not reach answers before.
Supervisors review juniors' research and reasoning, not only the answer.
who: Jansen & Company, Sasserath & Co., Finney Neill

title: Reusable planning blueprints that turn client data into a decision matrix
problem: An S-corporation election analysis for a sole proprietor was about a 10-hour project, and research on the old platform limited proactive client service.
approach: The firm builds a blueprint in Accordance that takes client financials, researches rules and produces a decision matrix and break-even point.
A tax shareholder says a 10-hour S-corporation election project becomes roughly two to two and a half hours (vendor-published).
A tax shareholder reviews the matrix and localised assumptions before it goes to the client.

title: Idea: planning-alternative ideation and anti-abuse screening of tax structures
problem: Idea, not a deployment: finding and testing planning alternatives across a large body of authority is slow and depends on a few senior people.
approach: Idea: a model proposes or completes planning strategies and probes them against authority; researchers report an apparently novel strategy from LLM reasoning.
No rate or count is published for adviser use (independent); the researchers frame the use for tax agencies.
A senior adviser tests every AI-proposed structure against economic substance and professional standards.

title: Idea: AI argues the other side, plays examiner or cross-checks a position
problem: Idea, not a deployment: positions are often tested only by the author and one reviewer, and one tool's confident answer can be wrong.
approach: Idea: ask a model to argue the opposite, list what an IRS examiner would flag, or run a second tool.
Disagreement between tools becomes a trigger for a deeper human check.
The adviser decides which objections are credible and checks both disagreements and consensus answers against primary authority.

title: Auditable tax computation: model translates rules, deterministic engine calculates
problem: Advice often turns on computations such as tax tables and eligibility, and language models alone get these wrong in ways that are hard to see.
approach: The model turns plain-text rules into inputs for a symbolic solver or tax engine that does the arithmetic, keeping a logic trace.
Johns Hopkins researchers tested this; the best model computed 32.35% of simplified returns correctly under the strict test (vendor-published).
The adviser reviews inputs, assumptions and the explanation of the calculation.

title: Document-grounded tax analysis of client agreements, trust documents and schedules
problem: Advisers read long operating agreements, trust and will documents and supporting schedules by hand before they can apply the tax rules.
approach: The adviser uploads a document; the tool summarises it and checks it against cited authority. Wright Ford Young uses it on agreements.
Jansen & Company wants to analyse trust and will documents; Wealth.com says its engine processed over 100,000 estate documents in 2025 (vendor-published).
The adviser checks the summary against the source document before relying on it.
who: Wright Ford Young, Jansen & Company, Wealth.com

title: Drafting technical memos, advice letters and client emails from researched authority
problem: Writing the memo, advice letter or client explanation after research takes days of associate time and varies between staff.
approach: The tool turns facts and authorities into a first draft the adviser edits; Blue J sells Tax Writing, used by Larson Gross.
One Stop CPA uses Blue J for research and ChatGPT for drafting; its CEO answered a deal question in two hours (self-reported).
Nelson Mullins is piloting platforms and says output resembles a junior associate's, not ready to send.
A named adviser edits, verifies every cited authority and approves each client-facing draft.
who: Blue J, KPMG, One Stop CPA, Larson Gross

title: Idea: AI support for tax opinions and in-house preliminary positions
problem: Idea, not a deployment: written advice must rest on verified facts and law, and corporates often defer to an expensive external opinion.
approach: Idea: AI assembles authorities, maps them to the facts and drafts the analysis, while a person decides the conclusion and signs.
A Kilpatrick Townsend alert says AI can help produce an opinion letter if the practitioner verifies the analysis and replaces fabricated authorities.
The signing professional owns the conclusion; opinion committee or second-partner review still applies.

title: Answering client questions during the call instead of researching and calling back
problem: Complex client questions meant telling the client we will research and call back, because complex research could consume most of a workday.
approach: With a cited research assistant open, the adviser looks up and tests an answer while the client is on the line.
A Director says the team can now get answers on a phone call, with 700+ queries per month tracked firm-wide (vendor-published).
The adviser decides what can be said live and what needs follow-up review.

title: Idea: client-facing tax question assistant that escalates to an adviser
problem: Idea, not a deployment: clients ask routine tax questions that consume adviser time, and many already ask general chatbots.
approach: Idea: a chatbot answers routine questions from the firm's approved content and routes nuanced or high-stakes ones to an adviser.
Australia's TPB lists tailored-advice chatbots as an AI capability practitioners may use; HMRC asks generative AI tax software to flag nuanced rules.
Fact-dependent or advice-level questions escalate to a qualified adviser.

title: Idea: triage AI-generated tax answers and citations that clients or opponents bring
problem: Idea, not a deployment: clients act on chatbot answers, and counterparties send AI-generated citations that may be wrong.
approach: Idea: run incoming material through the firm's own citation and consistency checks, and counsel clients to ask AI for primary sources.
In Clinco the IRS flagged nonexistent cases; in Harber the tribunal and HMRC found nine cited decisions did not exist.
The adviser reviews flagged material and its sources before adopting a position or responding.

title: Citation verification and an AI-use record as a standing review step
problem: AI can produce plausible but nonexistent authority, as in Clinco, and regulators expect practitioners to show how output was verified.
approach: Reviewers confirm every cited authority exists and supports the draft, and the file records the prompt, output, citations, verification and reviewer.
KPMG US M&A Tax says its human-in-the-loop model uses citations and hyperlinks to validate all AI outputs.
A second reviewer cross-checks authorities before a filing or memo goes out; the responsible partner signs off the record.
who: KPMG US, Wolters Kluwer, Aon adviser

title: Automated check that every cited authority exists and supports the point
problem: Fabricated or misdescribed citations reach client memos and court filings, and manual cite-checking of every authority is slow.
approach: A checker resolves every citation against authoritative sources and flags those that do not exist or do not support the point.
Damien Charlotin offers an automated reference checker, PelAIkan; it has no published error rates (vendor-published).
A person clears every flagged citation and reads the authorities that carry the argument.

title: M&A tax diligence: AI reviews purchase agreements, drafts a diligence report
problem: Transaction tax teams read long purchase agreements, research deal rules and write diligence reports under deadlines, leaving less time for structuring analysis.
approach: KPMG US M&A Tax describes four GenAI tools: research assistant, agreement review against baselines, diligence report drafting and a writing review assistant.
KPMG's web page says the firm is compressing weeks of tax analysis into minutes (self-reported).
Professionals add their own assessments, validate output against source documents and a senior reviewer signs.

title: Diligence agent reads the data room, drafts a cited tax risk assessment
problem: Tax diligence over entity structures, intercompany agreements and filings takes weeks of document analysis across entities and jurisdictions.
approach: V7 markets an agent that ingests financials, returns and agreements, maps entity structures, flags permanent establishment issues and returns a cited assessment.
V7's demo compares 3-4 weeks with 2-3 days, average time saved 90% (vendor-published).
The deal tax lead reviews the assessment before it informs price or structure.

title: Law-change monitoring that drafts client-specific impact notes for adviser review
problem: After major legislation advisers must track guidance across jurisdictions and explain the effect to each client, which is repetitive and urgent.
approach: A monitoring agent watches new law and guidance and drafts client impact notes; Bloomberg Tax describes an AI Assistant in Compliance Tracker.
KPMG's tax vice chair says building a client agent for changing regulations went from weeks to minutes with Claude Cowork (self-reported).
The adviser confirms each flagged change and its client impact before anything reaches the client.

title: Advisers co-build client-specific tax agents with clients on firm platforms
problem: Building an agent to help clients adjust to changing tax regulations used to take weeks and several tools.
approach: KPMG's Digital Gateway, built on Claude and announced 20 May 2026, lets professionals and clients build agentic workflows, starting with tax.
EY announced EY.ai Tax Labs and the Tax Agent Factory on 25 Nov 2025 to build and deploy agents with clients.
KPMG's tax vice chair says build time went from weeks to minutes (self-reported); checkpoints are not described in the sources.

title: Value-based and fixed-fee pricing as AI shortens research and drafting
problem: Hourly billing ties revenue to time AI removes, and IRS OPR says billing for manual time not spent may violate the fee rule.
approach: Firms test fixed monthly fees, project pricing and value-based models; Sasserath & Co. moved onboarding to fixed monthly fees where appropriate.
RKL is piloting an alternative pricing model, with several dozen new clients onboarded (self-reported); RSM US says it increasingly bills on value.
This is a pricing change, not an AI workflow; the engagement partner sets the fee basis.
who: Sasserath & Co., RKL, RSM US, PwC

title: Owner-facing S-election calculators and agent-built S corporation plans
problem: Owners want to know whether an S election saves tax for their business, and generic calculators handle only W-2 cases.
approach: Gelt launched AI calculators on 2025-12-29, including an S Corp calculator; Instead lists a workflow to build an S corporation tax plan.
Thomson Reuters says CoCounsel Tax can evaluate S corporation conversions against Checkpoint content, with citations.
Gelt describes the calculators as lead generation, with no conversion figure published (vendor-published); an adviser confirms facts and assumptions.

title: Planning opportunities mined from filed owner returns across the client book
problem: 93% of respondents to the 2026 AICPA tax software survey use no tool to review returns for planning opportunities.
approach: Intuit Tax Advisor generates strategies from ProConnect or Lacerte returns; Wolters Kluwer's CCH Axcess Advisor surfaces opportunities and drafts outreach.
Filed says its Tax Planner builds an evidence-based plan from the return; WCG says secure environments can already support plan comparisons.
The adviser confirms eligibility and substance before any strategy is proposed to the owner.

title: Idea: informed consent and verification rules for AI in estate planning
problem: Idea, not a deployment: estate-planning professionals are adopting AI, and ACTEC Fellows say hundreds of attorneys and judges have cited fabricated authority.
approach: Idea: tell clients the firm uses AI and how, get separate informed consent, verify every output against source and build competence first.
ACTEC Fellow Gerry Beyer recommends a separately signed provision.
The attorney or adviser verifies every AI output, and consent is obtained before AI touches client data.
